metadata.title: The effect of teacher collaboration on teachers' career well-being in China: A moderated mediation model of teacher self-efficacy and distributed leadership

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses secondary data from the 2018 TALIS, but the analysis is restricted to a TALIS Shanghai database sample of junior high school teachers (N=3159). The manuscript does not report the use of TALIS sampling/survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure, and it does not name any weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because the analysis is conducted with SPSS PROCESS macro (mediation/moderation with bootstrapping) rather than PV-based achievement modeling, the paper provides no guidance on weight application for complex survey design. Analysts using the original TALIS microdata should verify whether the Shanghai subsample retains TALIS design variables and, if so, consider applying appropriate complex-survey weights when estimating population-representative effects; however, this paper itself does not document such weighting.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study models teachers’ self-reported Likert-scale constructs (teacher collaboration, career well-being, self-efficacy, distributed leadership) rather than cognitive achievement outcomes with TALIS plausible values. As a result, plausible values are not applicable to the dependent variables used here. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap because missingness rules can affect mediation/moderation estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample consists of 3159 junior high school teachers from Shanghai, drawn from the TALIS Shanghai database (a designated sampling area within TALIS 2018). The paper does not report additional inclusion/exclusion filters beyond this Shanghai junior-high teacher restriction, and it does not specify any further task/module completion criteria or missing-data exclusions.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Mediation model (PROCESS Model 4): teacher collaboration → career well-being β=0.117 (p<0.001); direct effect TC → CWE=0.099 (95% CI excludes 0); indirect (TC → SE → CWE)=0.018 (95% CI excludes 0). Total effect R²=0.047 (R=0.216; F=38.496, p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, junior high teachers) the study leveraged teacher collaboration and teacher self-efficacy (with gender, teaching experience, and educational background as controls) to predict teachers’ career well-being, finding that teacher collaboration had a significant positive direct effect and an additional positive indirect effect through self-efficacy. This indicates that strengthening collaborative teacher practices and building teachers’ self-efficacy may improve career well-being, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Moderation model (PROCESS Model 59): teacher collaboration → self-efficacy β=0.166 (p<0.001); distributed leadership → self-efficacy β=0.066 (p<0.001); interaction TC × DL → self-efficacy β=0.066 (p<0.001). Model R²=0.114 (R=0.337; F=67.478, p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, junior high teachers) the study leveraged teacher collaboration and distributed leadership (with gender, teaching experience, and educational background as controls) to predict teachers’ self-efficacy, finding that collaboration was positively associated with self-efficacy and that distributed leadership significantly strengthened this relationship. This indicates that school-level leadership practices that distribute decision-making and responsibility can amplify the self-efficacy benefits of teacher collaboration, though causality cannot be established from the cross-sectional survey.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Moderation of direct and mediated paths (PROCESS Model 59): TC × DL → career well-being β=0.030 (p<0.05); self-efficacy × DL → career well-being β=0.020 (p>0.05, not significant). Moderated mediation: distributed leadership moderated the mediating effect of self-efficacy (Table 6 shows moderated mediation effects at E1/E2/E3 with BootLLCI/BootULCI not crossing 0 for higher DL levels). Simple slopes: TC → career well-being stronger at high DL (simple slope=0.047, t=3.839, p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Shanghai, junior high teachers) the study leveraged teacher collaboration, self-efficacy, and distributed leadership to predict career well-being, finding that distributed leadership significantly moderated the collaboration-to-career-well-being link and strengthened the self-efficacy mediation pathway (while the self-efficacy × distributed leadership interaction on career well-being was not significant). This indicates that policy and school practice should pair collaboration initiatives with distributed leadership structures to maximize improvements in teachers’ career well-being, while recognizing that the study’s design does not support causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: This Acta Psychologica study uses TALIS 2018 data restricted to a Shanghai subsample of 3159 junior high school teachers. Rather than machine learning, the authors estimate mediation and moderated mediation using SPSS PROCESS (Model 4 for mediation; Model 59 for moderation) with bias-corrected percentile bootstrapping (5000 replications) and control variables (gender, teaching experience, educational background). Teacher collaboration shows a significant positive association with both career well-being and self-efficacy (e.g., TC → CWE β=0.117, p<0.001; TC → SE β=0.166, p<0.001), and self-efficacy significantly mediates the TC–career well-being relationship (indirect effect=0.018, 95% CI excludes 0). Distributed leadership further moderates the collaboration effects (TC × DL → career well-being β=0.030, p<0.05; TC × DL → self-efficacy β=0.066, p<0.001) and moderates the mediation pathway, with stronger effects at high distributed leadership. Limitations include cross-sectional data and no documented missing-data handling or survey-weight application.
